title: Illumina library prep
subtitle: From genomic DNA to a sequencer-ready library, one step at a time.
objectives: Draw and label a finished Illumina library molecule.
Explain what each prep step does and why it is needed.
Name the main ways protocols differ and what each choice changes.
Recognise common library-prep failures from their QC signatures.

steps.title: Starting material
steps.caption: Ideally, we would start with high-molecular-weight DNA, although degraded DNA can still work for standard Illumina library preps. The quality of the DNA is dependent on how well the tissue was preserved and the quantity is dependent on the tissue type and amount. Different extraction methods can have different efficacies but the most important factor is how well the tissues have been preserved.

extractionMethods.label: Column-based (silica membrane)
extractionMethods.summary: DNA selectively binds a silica membrane in a chaotropic salt buffer, impurities wash through, then DNA elutes in a low-salt buffer or water.
extractionMethods.detail: Lysed sample is mixed with a chaotropic salt buffer (e.g. guanidinium) that makes DNA bind a silica membrane in a spin column, while proteins, salts and other contaminants pass through during wash steps; purified DNA is then eluted off the membrane. It's fast and scales well with manual or automated (robotic) processing, and needs no hazardous organic solvents, but the membrane's binding capacity can shear or exclude very large fragments, and repeated washes can reduce yield from low-input samples.

extractionMethods.label: Magnetic bead-based
extractionMethods.summary: Paramagnetic beads reversibly bind DNA in a binding buffer, are pulled out of solution with a magnet, washed, then DNA is released in an elution buffer.
extractionMethods.detail: Similar chemistry to silica columns, but the solid phase is a suspension of paramagnetic beads instead of a fixed membrane: beads are mixed directly into the lysate, bound DNA is captured against a magnetic rack, unbound contaminants are washed away, and the beads are resuspended in elution buffer to release the DNA. It's the easiest method to automate in a 96-well format and handles very high-molecular-weight DNA more gently than a column, but the reagents tend to cost more per sample than columns.

extractionMethods.label: Phenol-chloroform extraction
extractionMethods.summary: A classic manual method: DNA partitions into the aqueous phase of a phenol-chloroform mixture, leaving proteins and lipids behind in the organic phase.
extractionMethods.detail: Lysed sample is mixed with phenol and chloroform; after centrifugation it separates into an upper aqueous phase holding the DNA and a lower organic phase holding denatured proteins and lipids, with cellular debris trapped at the interface. The aqueous phase is transferred off and the DNA is concentrated by ethanol precipitation. It yields very high-molecular-weight, high-purity DNA and needs no specialised kit, but it's slow, hands-on, and uses hazardous, toxic organic solvents that need careful handling and disposal.

steps.title: Input QC
steps.caption: The DNA then needs to be quantified and checked on a gel electrophoresis. Intact DNA would require a lot of shearing while degraded DNA might require little to no shearing. It may also be important to normalize the DNA amount/concentration to match the requirements of the specific library prep protocol.

quantMethods.label: Spectrophotometry (NanoDrop)
quantMethods.summary: Shines UV light through a small sample droplet and measures how much is absorbed at 260 nm.
quantMethods.detail: A drop of sample bridges two fibre-optic pedestals. Light at 260 nm, where nucleic acids absorb, and 280 nm, where proteins absorb, passes through the drop to a detector. The A260/280 ratio flags protein contamination — a value near 1.8 is considered clean DNA, and lower values suggest leftover protein. The A260/230 ratio flags contamination from salts, phenol and other extraction reagents — clean DNA is usually between about 2.0 and 2.2. That makes it a useful, reagent-free first look at how much contaminant is in a sample, but it measures all nucleic acids and contaminants together, so it tends to overestimate the DNA actually available to sequence.

quantMethods.label: Fluorometry (Qubit)
quantMethods.summary: Uses a dye that only lights up once bound to double-stranded DNA, then measures that glow.
quantMethods.detail: The sample is mixed with a dye that fluoresces only once bound to double-stranded DNA. A targeted light source excites the dye, and a detector measures the emitted fluorescence, which scales with dsDNA concentration. Because it only reports double-stranded DNA — not RNA, single-stranded DNA or contaminants — it's the more accurate method for estimating how much DNA you actually have, so its values are the ones to use when quantifying DNA for library prep.

steps.title: Fragmentation
steps.caption: DNA is sheared into the intended target size. The more intact the DNA, the more shearing needs to occur. Ideally, all samples should have roughly the same size distribution.

fragMethods.label: Sonication
fragMethods.summary: Focused ultrasonic waves shear DNA through rapid bubble formation and collapse.
fragMethods.detail: A probe or ultrasonic bath generates high-frequency sound waves in the sample, forming microscopic bubbles that collapse violently (cavitation) and physically shear the DNA. Power, duration and number of cycles set the target fragment size. It gives fairly random, reproducible breakpoints and a tunable size distribution, but needs dedicated equipment (e.g. a Covaris instrument) and can heat the sample if not controlled.

fragMethods.label: Enzymatic shearing
fragMethods.summary: A cocktail of enzymes nicks and cuts the DNA at semi-random sites.
fragMethods.detail: A mix of enzymes — typically a nicking enzyme paired with a nuclease that cuts opposite each nick — fragments the DNA during a short, temperature-controlled incubation. It needs no specialised equipment beyond a thermocycler, and incubation time sets the fragment size, but the enzymes can show some sequence bias in where they cut.

fragMethods.label: Tagmentation
fragMethods.summary: A transposase enzyme cuts the DNA and inserts sequencing adapters in the same step.
fragMethods.detail: A transposase (commonly Tn5) loaded with adapter sequences simultaneously cuts the DNA and ligates an adapter at each cut site. Because fragmentation and adapter attachment happen together, it skips the separate end-repair and ligation steps entirely and needs very little input DNA — but the insertion sites aren't fully random, which can introduce some sequence bias, and it's more sensitive to getting the DNA-to-enzyme ratio right.

failures.label: Under-sheared
failures.mechanism: Too little time, power or enzyme activity leaves fragments larger than the target size.
failures.fingerprint: The size-distribution trace shifts and broadens toward larger fragments. Bead clean-up then discards more of the library trying to pull the upper size cut-off back in, lowering yield.
failures.mitigation: Fixable — re-shear the sample for longer, or run another round of fragmentation.

failures.label: Over-sheared
failures.mechanism: Too much time, power or enzyme activity leaves fragments smaller than the target size.
failures.fingerprint: The size-distribution trace shifts toward very small fragments. Many are lost at the lower bead clean-up cut-off, and the surviving inserts — shorter than the read length — let reads sequence into the adapter.
failures.mitigation: Not fixable — the only option is to re-prep from fresh input DNA with gentler fragmentation conditions.

failures.label: GC bias (tagmentation)
failures.mechanism: Tn5 transposase doesn't cut DNA uniformly — it prefers certain sequence motifs, so some regions fragment more readily than others.
failures.fingerprint: Coverage becomes uneven across the genome: GC-rich and AT-rich regions are systematically under- or over-represented, seen as a tilted coverage-vs-GC-content curve instead of a flat line.
failures.mitigation: Switch to sonication or enzymatic shearing where even coverage matters, or correct for it computationally during analysis.

fragQC.title: Fragmentation QC (optional)
fragQC.caption: To ensure optimal size distribution, run the sheared DNA on a gel electrophoresis or an electropherogram then adjust the fragmentation protocol accordingly. Different starting quality DNA as well as different species may require different fragmentation profiles.

steps.title: End repair and A-tailing
steps.caption: Shearing leaves jagged ends. A DNA polymerase is used to fill in the complementary bases and a polynucleotide kinase (PNK) is used to add a phosphate group to the 5' end so they can be ligated to adapters. In the same reaction, an A base is added to the 3' end which allows the T overhang of the adapters to attach during the next step.

steps.title: Adapter ligation
steps.caption: Illumina adapters are then ligated on both ends of each DNA fragment. Illumina adapters carry all the information the sequencer needs: flow-cell binding sites, primer sites, and indexes. Adapters are often Y-shaped with a T-overhang so that it specifically binds to the A overhang and does not allow for more than one adapter to ligate.

indexMethods.label: Single indexing
indexMethods.summary: Each sample gets one index sequence on just one adapter end (typically i7); samples are distinguished by that single barcode alone.
indexMethods.detail: Only one of the two adapter ends carries a sample-specific index, so demultiplexing depends on correctly reading just that one barcode. It needs fewer unique index sequences and a simpler adapter inventory for small pools, but a misread or hopped index can't be cross-checked against anything else, so there's no way to catch or filter a misassigned read -- it's rarely used for larger, highly-multiplexed pools.

indexMethods.label: Combinatorial dual indexing (CDI)
indexMethods.summary: Each sample gets a pair of indexes (i5 + i7), but the individual index sequences are reused across many samples in different combinations.
indexMethods.detail: A relatively small set of i5 and i7 sequences are combined pairwise, so the same i5 sequence might pair with several different i7 sequences across the pool, and vice versa. It needs far fewer unique index sequences to multiplex many samples, keeping the adapter inventory small, but if one of the two indexes hops onto a different molecule, the resulting pair can still match a different real sample in the pool -- so a hopped read is sometimes misassigned rather than caught.

indexMethods.label: Unique dual indexing (UDI)
indexMethods.summary: Each sample gets its own unique i5 and i7 pair that is never reused anywhere else in the pool, in either position.
indexMethods.detail: Every i5 and i7 sequence in the pool is unique to one sample and never appears in any other sample's pair, so if either index hops onto a different molecule, the resulting combination doesn't match any real sample and the read can be identified and filtered out during demultiplexing rather than silently misassigned. It needs a larger, non-reusable set of index adapters -- more expensive to stock for large pools -- but it's the standard recommendation whenever index-hopping risk matters, such as on patterned flow cells.

failures.label: Adapter dimers
failures.mechanism: When adapter is in excess relative to insert DNA — or insert input is very low — two Y-adapters can ligate directly to each other instead of each finding an insert.
failures.fingerprint: Produces a short, sharp peak around 120 bp, smaller than any real insert. It PCR-amplifies efficiently and can dominate the sequenced library, wasting reads on empty adapter-adapter products with no insert at all.
failures.mitigation: Increase the insert:adapter molar ratio before ligation, and run an extra, tighter bead clean-up afterward to pull the short dimer peak out of the library.

failures.label: Chimeric ligation
failures.mechanism: Too much insert DNA relative to adapter, or incomplete A-tailing, lets two blunt insert fragments ligate to each other before an adapter does — stitching two unrelated genomic regions into one molecule.
failures.fingerprint: Looks just like a longer real fragment, so the size trace alone can't tell them apart. It only surfaces after sequencing, as reads that appear to span an impossible genomic fusion or structural variant.
failures.mitigation: Keep insert DNA at the protocol's recommended concentration for ligation, and confirm A-tailing went to completion — a clean A/T-specific overhang prevents blunt-end insert-to-insert joining.

steps.title: Library PCR
steps.caption: PCR completes or enriches full-length molecules and raises the yield. The first cycle is special: each original strand only has a primer site at one end, so polymerase must copy all the way across to create a proper binding site at the other end. From the second cycle on, primers anneal at both ends and every molecule doubles. Each cycle adds bias.

ampMethods.label: Standard PCR amplification
ampMethods.summary: A few cycles of PCR amplify the adapter-ligated library before sequencing, using primers matching the P5/P7 regions shown here.
ampMethods.detail: The ligated library is amplified with primers matching the P5 and P7 regions of the adapters, producing many copies of each fragment and raising the overall yield enough to sequence from a small amount of starting material. It works from low-input or lower-quality DNA where there isn't enough material to sequence directly, but every extra cycle introduces some duplication and amplification bias (see 'Break it' below).

ampMethods.label: PCR-free library prep
ampMethods.summary: Skips amplification entirely -- enough adapter-ligated library is carried straight into sequencing without ever being copied by a polymerase.
ampMethods.detail: Rather than amplifying the ligated library, enough input DNA is used up front that the post-ligation material alone is sufficient to load onto the flow cell. Because no PCR ever happens, there are no PCR duplicates and no GC/AT amplification bias, giving the most even, representative coverage across the genome. It needs considerably more, higher-quality starting DNA than a PCR-amplified protocol can get away with, so it isn't an option for low-input, degraded or precious samples.

failures.label: Over-amplification
failures.mechanism: Running too many PCR cycles, or starting from very little input DNA, means the same original molecules get copied over and over. Eventually most of what's being amplified is PCR duplicates of a few starting molecules, not new, unique fragments.
failures.fingerprint: Doesn't show up on a size trace — duplicate molecules are the same length as everything else. It only appears after sequencing, as a high fraction of reads mapping to the exact same start and end position.
failures.mitigation: Use fewer PCR cycles, start with more input DNA, or add unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) before amplification so duplicates can be identified and removed computationally.

failures.label: GC/AT bias
failures.mechanism: DNA polymerase has a harder time denaturing and copying through extremely GC-rich or AT-rich stretches, so those regions amplify less efficiently than the rest of the genome each cycle.
failures.fingerprint: Coverage becomes uneven across the genome: GC-rich and AT-rich regions are systematically under-represented, the same tilted coverage-vs-GC-content curve seen from tagmentation bias, but caused by the polymerase rather than the fragmentation enzyme.
failures.mitigation: Use fewer PCR cycles (or a PCR-free library prep when input allows), and a polymerase/buffer formulated for high-GC amplification.

libraryQC.title: Library QC (optional)
libraryQC.caption: The quality of individual libraries can be assessed using gel electrophoresis, electropherograms (Bioanalyzer or TapeStation), or qPCR and quantified using a Fluorometer (Qubit). The gel electrophoresis is a rough check to see if the PCR worked and if the fragments are roughly the correct size. The electropherogram would give you a more accurate size distribution while the qPCR will actually give you the number of molecules. The latter methods are more expensive and will not scale well when doing many libraries. The quantification is useful if you want to normalize the library concentration and pool them more evenly but this is also time consuming for many samples. If the protocol has been optimized such that each library yields roughly the same amount, then the QC step can be skipped and libraries pooled using equal volumes rather than normalized at this step.

steps.title: Normalize
steps.caption: To ensure that the correct amounts of library is being added to the pool both the quantity and size distribution of the library should be normalized. The size distribution can be normalized either by a double-sided bead clean-up or gel excision (ex. using a BluePippin). The quantity measured using a fluorometer should be used  when calculating the exact amounts for pooling. If the protocol has been optimized and yielding similar amounts and size distributions, this step may be skipped.

normalizeMethods.label: Double-sided bead size selection
normalizeMethods.summary: Two rounds of magnetic-bead binding at different bead:sample ratios trim both size extremes.
normalizeMethods.detail: A low bead ratio is added first and binds only the largest fragments, which are discarded; more beads are then added to the remaining supernatant to capture the target size range, and the leftover small-fragment supernatant is discarded. It needs no specialized equipment beyond a magnetic rack, but the exact size cut-offs are only approximate and depend on the bead ratios used.

normalizeMethods.label: Gel excision
normalizeMethods.summary: The library is run on a gel (or an automated cassette like a BluePippin) and the band at the target size is physically cut out and purified.
normalizeMethods.detail: Because it separates and recovers a specific size directly from a real gel image, it gives a tighter, more precise size window than bead selection, and automated systems like the BluePippin make it reproducible across many samples. It takes more time and specialized equipment, and manual excision adds a contamination risk if not done carefully.

normalizeMethods.label: Enzymatic normalization
normalizeMethods.summary: An enzyme mix that saturates at a fixed DNA amount selectively degrades the excess material in over-concentrated samples.
normalizeMethods.detail: Libraries are incubated with a double-stranded-DNA-binding protein and nuclease pair that protects only a defined amount of DNA before saturating, so anything above that amount gets degraded -- bringing all samples down toward the same final concentration without needing to measure each one individually beforehand. It's fast and scales well across many samples, but it can only trim down overly concentrated libraries, not boost ones that started too dilute.

steps.title: Pool and final QC
steps.caption: Pool libraries according to the desired ratio. Libraries can be pooled into one large pool or multiple smaller pools but it is crucial that no two libraries share the same index

failures.label: Index hopping
failures.mechanism: Free, unextended adapter or index primer carried over in the pool can misprime during cluster generation -- especially on patterned flow cells with ExAmp chemistry -- attaching the wrong sample's index to a read.
failures.fingerprint: Doesn't show up on a size trace -- hopped molecules are the normal library size. It only appears after demultiplexing, as a small fraction of reads for every index combination showing up under every other sample in the pool.
failures.mitigation: Use unique dual indexes (UDI) instead of combinatorial dual indexes, so a hopped read can't be demultiplexed as a false real sample, and keep free adapter/primer carryover low with a clean final bead clean-up.

failures.label: Adapter annealing
failures.mechanism: Pooled libraries can partially denature during storage or handling, and the single-stranded adapter ends re-anneal to each other instead of staying apart, chaining separate molecules together into much larger complexes.
failures.fingerprint: The DNA fragment distribution shows a much larger fragment size than expected, since the annealed complexes run as one much bigger apparent molecule rather than the true library size.
failures.mitigation: Run the pool through a couple of cycles of PCR -- it denatures the annealed complexes and re-synthesizes clean, correctly-sized double-stranded library molecules.

finalQC.title: Final QC
finalQC.caption: Prior to sending the sample for sequencing, a final quantification and size check should be run using a flourometer and an electropherogram, respectively. If the fragment size is still not as desired, you can run the pooled sample through a BluePippin. It is more important that there are no large fragments being sequenced as it can disrupt the process.
